segments.say: There's a moment in Hana's book, about halfway through, when the woman in the story says something cruel to her sister, and then, alone in her room, cries about it. Hana felt that. She understood exactly why the woman had lashed out, and exactly why she regretted it. For a few pages, Hana was inside another person's head, feeling her mixed-up feelings from the inside.

The Canadian psychologist and novelist Keith Oatley has described fiction as a kind of simulation. A bit like a flight simulator, but for the social world. When we read a novel, we practice imagining what other people think and feel, why they do what they do, and what might happen next between them. And practice, the idea goes, might make us a little better at it in real life.

Psychologists have a name for the skill being practiced here. It's called theory of mind. It's our ability to understand that other people have their own beliefs, desires and feelings, which can differ from ours. It's what lets you guess that a friend is upset from a pause in her voice, or understand why a colleague is being prickly before a big meeting.

In 2006, a team at the University of Toronto, including Raymond Mar and Keith Oatley, published a study with a playful title, Bookworms versus nerds. Instead of asking people how much they read, which people often get wrong, they gave them a list of names and asked which ones they recognized as authors. Some names were fiction writers, some wrote non-fiction, and some were made up.

show.what: Adults' exposure to fiction and non-fiction was measured by how many authors' names they recognized. People who recognized more fiction authors tended to do better on tests of empathy and social understanding.

segments.say: They found that people who recognized more fiction authors, a rough sign of reading more fiction, tended to score better on tests of social understanding. One of these tests involved looking at photographs of just the eyes of different people, and choosing which feeling each pair of eyes showed. Readers of non-fiction didn't show the same pattern.

But there's an obvious question here, and the researchers asked it themselves. Maybe reading fiction doesn't make people more socially attuned. Maybe people who are already socially attuned are more drawn to fiction. A study like this can show a link, but not which way it runs.

So in 2013, two researchers at the New School for Social Research in New York, David Kidd and Emanuele Castano, tried a bolder test. Published in the journal Science, it suggested something remarkable. People who were asked to read a short passage of literary fiction did better afterward on theory of mind tests than people who read popular fiction, non-fiction, or nothing.

Kidd and Castano's study got enormous attention. Newspapers around the world reported that reading literary fiction could improve empathy. And it's a lovely idea. But it was also a bold claim. Could reading just one short story really change, in a measurable way, how well you read other people?

In 2016, a group of researchers, led by Maria Eugenia Panero, tried to repeat Kidd and Castano's experiments carefully, with a much larger group of participants. Their paper was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. And they did not find the effect. Reading one passage of literary fiction did not reliably improve theory of mind scores.

show.what: Researchers repeated the 2013 single-passage experiments with a much larger sample. They did not find that one passage of literary fiction improved scores on theory of mind tests.

segments.say: This is how science is supposed to work, even if it can feel disappointing. An exciting result was published, other scientists tried to reproduce it, and it didn't hold up in its strongest form. Other replication attempts have also found mixed results. So the claim that a single story improves your empathy on the spot is, at best, uncertain.

show.text: A lovely idea still has to be tested. Sometimes, it doesn't survive the test.

segments.say: What about the longer-term link, between being a lifelong reader of fiction and social understanding? That one has held up better. Several later studies, including a review that combined many results, have found a small positive link between reading fiction and measures of social understanding. Small, and still hard to interpret fully. But present.

So here's where the evidence stands. Fiction can be thought of as a simulation of social life. Lifelong fiction readers show a small link with social understanding. A single short story doesn't seem to produce a reliable effect. And the direction of the link, whether reading builds understanding or understanding draws people to reading, is still unclear.

show.title: Fiction and other minds
items: Lifelong readers show a small link

segments.say: What we can say, gently, is this. Spending time inside other minds, even imagined ones, is at least a chance to practice. It's a safe place to feel what it might be like to be someone else. Whether it changes us much, and how quickly, is still being studied. But many readers would tell you it has changed them, and that's worth something too.

Hana, reading about the woman and her sister, thinks for a moment about her own sister, Lise, and a sharp text she sent her last week about a birthday plan. She hadn't really thought about how it might have landed. The book didn't tell her anything new about Lise. But it gave her a moment to imagine Lise's side.

Perhaps that's how fiction's influence works, if it does. Not in one big leap, but in small moments like this. A character makes you think of someone you know, and for a second you see them from a slightly different angle. Hana makes a note to call Lise tomorrow.

Hana's book, like most books, has a shape. Things get worse for the woman, then a little better, then much worse, and Hana suspects that somewhere near the end, they'll get better again. Is that shape just this author's choice? Or do stories tend to follow a small number of shapes? A team of researchers once used computers to find out.
